prompt.6-12: Daniel Freeman filed one of the first Homestead Act claims in 1863. Where was his land?
prompt.adult: Daniel Freeman's 1863 claim, among the first under the Homestead Act, is now a national historical park. Where is it?

choices.why: Abilene became famous as a cattle-drive railhead in the late 1860s, not for the first homestead claim.
Many settlers homesteaded in Dakota Territory, but the claim tied to the act's first day was in Nebraska.
Denver grew out of the 1858 gold rush, a mining boom rather than farm claims.

explanation: Freeman filed at the Brownville land office just after midnight on January 1, 1863. His land on Cub Creek near Beatrice is now Homestead National Historical Park.

prompt.6-12: Which event is connected to the land near Beatrice, Nebraska?

choices.text: One of the first claims under the Homestead Act is filed (1863)
The golden spike completes the transcontinental railroad (1869)
choices.why: That happened at Promontory Summit, Utah.
Black Sunday hit hardest in the southern Plains, especially the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles.

choices.text: Lewis and Clark hold their first council with the Otoe and Missouria (1804)
choices.why: That council was at "Council Bluff" on the Missouri River, north of present-day Omaha, near Fort Calhoun.

explanation: Homestead National Historical Park near Beatrice preserves Daniel Freeman's 1863 claim, one of the first under the Homestead Act.

prompt.adult: Black homesteaders founded the Sandhills community of DeWitty under the Kinkaid Act. In which state was it?

choices.why: Nicodemus, Kansas, founded in 1877, is the best-known Black homestead town, but it is not DeWitty.
Oklahoma had many all-Black towns, such as Boley, but the Kinkaid Act applied only to western Nebraska.
Dearfield, Colorado, was a Black homestead colony founded in 1910, but DeWitty was in Nebraska.

explanation: The 1904 Kinkaid Act offered 640-acre homesteads in western Nebraska. DeWitty, in Cherry County, was the state's largest rural Black settlement.

prompt.6-12: In 1879, a federal judge ruled that Ponca chief Standing Bear was a "person" under the law. Where was the case heard?

choices.why: The case never reached the Supreme Court. It was decided in federal district court in Omaha.
Fort Laramie is famous for treaties signed in 1851 and 1868, not for this case.
That is where the Ponca had been forced to move. Standing Bear was arrested after leaving it and tried in Omaha.

explanation: Standing Bear was held at Fort Omaha, and Judge Elmer Dundy heard his habeas corpus case in federal court in Omaha in May 1879.

prompt.6-12: Which event happened in Omaha, Nebraska?

choices.text: Standing Bear wins a ruling that a Native American is a person under the law (1879)
Sitting Bull surrenders to the US Army (1881)
choices.why: Sitting Bull surrendered at Fort Buford, in present-day North Dakota.

choices.text: The Battle of the Little Bighorn (1876)
choices.why: That battle took place in Montana Territory.
Wounded Knee is in South Dakota, on the Pine Ridge Reservation.

explanation: Standing Bear v. Crook was decided in Omaha in 1879, a landmark moment for Native American legal rights.

prompt.6-12: Standing Bear promised to bury his son in the Ponca homeland. That homeland is along which Nebraska river?

choices.why: The Platte crosses central Nebraska and guided the Oregon Trail. The Ponca homeland was farther north and east.
The Republican runs through southern Nebraska and northern Kansas.
The Arkansas flows through Indian Territory, where the Ponca were sent, not their home.

explanation: The Ponca homeland is where the Niobrara meets the Missouri River in northeast Nebraska.

prompt.6-12: Where did the Second Continental Congress adopt the Declaration of Independence in July 1776?

choices.why: Boston was the scene of the Tea Party and early protests, but Congress met in Philadelphia.
Virginia's convention met there in May 1776 and urged independence, but the Declaration was adopted in Philadelphia.
New York was the first capital under the Constitution in 1789, where Washington took the oath of office.

explanation: Congress met in the Pennsylvania State House, now called Independence Hall, in Philadelphia.

prompt.6-12: Which event happened in Philadelphia?

choices.text: Congress approves the Declaration of Independence (1776)

choices.why: Washington crossed about 30 miles upstream at McConkey's Ferry to attack Trenton, New Jersey.
That battle was fought in Charlestown, next to Boston.
Yorktown is in Virginia, on Chesapeake Bay.

explanation: The Declaration of Independence was debated and approved at the Pennsylvania State House in Philadelphia.

prompt.6-12: In 1869, the Central Pacific and Union Pacific railroads met to finish the first transcontinental railroad. Where?

choices.why: Omaha was where the Union Pacific started building west.
Sacramento was where the Central Pacific started building east.
Ogden became the main junction city afterward, but the ceremony was held at Promontory Summit, northwest of Ogden.

explanation: The golden spike ceremony took place at Promontory Summit on May 10, 1869.

prompt.6-12: Omaha, Nebraska, was the starting point for which project?

choices.text: The Union Pacific's half of the transcontinental railroad

choices.why: The Pony Express started in St. Joseph, Missouri, in 1860.
Most Oregon Trail travelers left from Missouri towns such as Independence.
Lewis and Clark set out from near St. Louis, Missouri, in 1804.

explanation: The Union Pacific broke ground in Omaha in 1863 and built west until meeting the Central Pacific in Utah in 1869.

prompt.6-12: In 1955, Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her bus seat. In what city?

choices.why: Birmingham was the site of a major 1963 campaign and the 16th Street Baptist Church bombing.
The 1965 voting rights marches started in Selma and ended in Montgomery.
Greensboro is known for the 1960 lunch counter sit-ins.

explanation: Parks was arrested in Montgomery on December 1, 1955, which sparked the 381-day bus boycott.

prompt.6-12: Which event took place in Montgomery, Alabama?

choices.text: A 381-day boycott of the city's segregated buses (1955-1956)
Brown v. Board of Education begins (1951)
choices.why: The Brown case began in Topeka, Kansas.

choices.text: The Little Rock Nine enter Central High School (1957)
choices.why: Central High School is in Little Rock, Arkansas.
That march took place in Washington, D.C.

explanation: The Montgomery Bus Boycott lasted from December 1955 to December 1956 and ended segregation on the city's buses.

prompt.adult: Fifteen-year-old Claudette Colvin refused to give up her bus seat nine months before Rosa Parks did. Where?

choices.why: Baton Rouge held an earlier bus boycott in 1953, but Colvin's arrest happened in Montgomery.
Tallahassee's bus boycott began in 1956, inspired by Montgomery's.
Atlanta was Martin Luther King Jr.'s hometown, but Colvin lived and was arrested in Montgomery.

explanation: Colvin was arrested in Montgomery in March 1955 and later became a plaintiff in Browder v. Gayle, the case that ended bus segregation there.

prompt.6-12: Where did Apollo 11 launch on its way to the first crewed Moon landing?

choices.why: Houston was home to Mission Control, which guided the flight once it left the launch tower.
The Saturn V rocket was developed in Huntsville, but it launched from Florida.
White Sands was used for rocket and engine testing, not crewed launches.

explanation: Apollo 11 lifted off from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center on July 16, 1969.

prompt.6-12: Which event began on Florida's Atlantic coast at Kennedy Space Center?

choices.text: The Apollo 11 mission to the Moon (1969)
The Wright brothers' first powered flight (1903)
choices.why: That flight took place at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.
That test was at the Trinity Site in New Mexico.
The Soviet Union launched Sputnik from Baikonur, in present-day Kazakhstan.

explanation: Apollo 11 launched from Kennedy Space Center, where rockets head east over the ocean.

prompt.6-12: Which of these happened near the town of Rashid (Rosetta) in Egypt?
prompt.adult: Which of these happened near Rashid (Rosetta), Egypt?

choices.text: French soldiers uncover a stone that unlocks Egyptian hieroglyphs (1799)

choices.why: The canal opened about 150 km to the east, at Port Said.
The Great Pyramid is at Giza, near Cairo.

choices.text: The Camp David Accords are signed (1978)
choices.why: They were signed at Camp David in Maryland, in the United States.

explanation: The Rosetta Stone was found near Rashid in the Nile Delta in July 1799.

prompt.6-12: Where was the Rosetta Stone discovered in 1799?

choices.text: Near Rashid, in Egypt's Nile Delta

choices.why: Giza is home to the pyramids and the Sphinx, not the Rosetta Stone.
Luxor is near the Valley of the Kings, where Tutankhamun's tomb was found in 1922.
The stone has been displayed in London's British Museum since 1802, but it was found in Egypt.

explanation: French soldiers found the stone while rebuilding a fort near Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta.

prompt.6-12: In November 1989, crowds crossed a wall that had divided their city for 28 years. Which city?

choices.why: Moscow was the Soviet capital, but it was never divided by a wall.
Prague's Velvet Revolution also happened in November 1989, but the city was never divided by a wall.
The Warsaw Pact was named for this city, but Warsaw was not split by a wall.

explanation: The Berlin Wall surrounded West Berlin from 1961 until its checkpoints opened on November 9, 1989.

prompt.6-12: Which event took place in Berlin?

choices.text: Border guards open the wall's checkpoints (1989)
The Treaty of Versailles is signed (1919)
choices.why: It was signed at the Palace of Versailles, near Paris, France.

choices.text: The end of the Soviet Union is announced (1991)
choices.why: Gorbachev resigned and the Soviet Union dissolved in Moscow.
Churchill gave that speech in Fulton, Missouri.

explanation: On the night of November 9, 1989, crowds pushed through Berlin's checkpoints, and the wall effectively fell.

prompt.6-12: Around 1450, the Inca emperor Pachacuti had a royal estate built high in the Andes mountains. What is it called today?

choices.why: Cusco was the Inca capital, about 75 km (47 miles) southeast of Machu Picchu.
Tenochtitlan was the Aztec capital, where Mexico City stands today.
Chichén Itzá is a Maya city on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula.

explanation: Machu Picchu sits on a ridge above the Urubamba River and was likely built as Pachacuti's royal estate.

prompt.6-12: Which event is connected to Machu Picchu?

choices.text: A 1911 expedition, guided by local farmers, makes the site famous worldwide
Francisco Pizarro captures the Inca ruler Atahualpa (1532)
choices.why: Atahualpa was captured at Cajamarca, in northern Peru.

choices.text: The Spanish found the city of Lima (1535)
choices.why: Lima is on Peru's Pacific coast, far from the mountains.

choices.text: Pilots spot the Nazca Lines from the air (1920s-1930s)
choices.why: The Nazca Lines are in the coastal desert of southern Peru.

explanation: Hiram Bingham reached Machu Picchu in 1911 with help from local guides, and his photographs brought it international fame.

prompt.6-12: Emperor Shah Jahan built a white marble tomb for his wife, Mumtaz Mahal. In which city?

choices.why: Shah Jahan also built the Red Fort in Delhi, but the Taj Mahal is in Agra.
Istanbul is known for Ottoman landmarks such as the Blue Mosque.
Persian buildings in cities like Isfahan influenced the Taj's style, but it was built in India.

explanation: The Taj Mahal stands on the south bank of the Yamuna River in Agra.

prompt.6-12: Which event is connected to Agra, India?

choices.text: A Mughal emperor builds the Taj Mahal (1632-1653)

choices.why: The Salt March went from Ahmedabad to Dandi, in the state of Gujarat.

choices.text: India celebrates independence at the Red Fort (1947)
choices.why: Prime Minister Nehru raised the flag at the Red Fort in Delhi.
Angkor Wat is in Cambodia.

explanation: Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in Agra as a tomb for Mumtaz Mahal.
